topic.title: Christian critiques of Islam
topic.thesis: Do the most common Christian arguments against Islam withstand the strongest documented counters?
topic.scope: This map steelmans popular Christian apologetic critiques, then pairs each with responses already present in Muslim scholarship, classical tafsir, and academic literature. It does not declare a winner.
method: One precise claim per node — no slogans
Tag the disagreement type: fact, history, definition, theology, or ethics
Attach receipts (primary texts, scholars, peer-reviewed work)
Name the crux: what would need to be true for this fork to close

arguments.title: Crucifixion denial vs historical consensus

christian.claim: If Jesus was historically crucified, and the Qur'an denies that event, then the Qur'an's historical reliability on Jesus fails at a high-stakes point.
christian.case: Mainstream Christian apologetics (e.g. William Lane Craig) treat Jesus' crucifixion as among the most secure facts about Jesus. Non-Christian sources such as Tacitus (Annals 15.44) and Josephus also report Jesus' execution. Bart Ehrman, a non-Christian critical scholar, calls the crucifixion "rock-bottom certain." Qur'an 4:157–158 is read as denying that Jesus was crucified, which would place Islam against the historical record.

receipts.label: Qur'an 4:157–158
receipts.note: Key text: they did not kill him, nor crucify him, but it was made to appear so…

receipts.label: Craig — Reasonable Faith Q&A
receipts.note: Argues Islamic denial is the Achilles' heel given historical consensus.

receipts.label: Bart Ehrman blog
receipts.note: States crucifixion is historically certain and at odds with standard Islamic belief.

receipts.label: Tacitus, Annals 15.44
receipts.note: Roman source referring to Christus executed under Pontius Pilate.

response.claim: Either (A) 4:157 denies Jewish agency/boast rather than the event itself, or (B) God rescued Jesus while allowing an apparent crucifixion, so public historical memory need not equal metaphysical outcome.
response.case: Muslim responses are not monolithic. Majority Sunni tafsir (Tabari, Zamakhshari) develops substitution narratives. A minority scholarly line (some Isma'ili readings; Todd Lawson) argues the Qur'an denies the Jews' successful claim, not necessarily that a crucifixion-looking event occurred. Some Muslim writers distinguish what appeared historically from what God actually did — absorbing historical consensus without conceding Christian soteriology.

receipts.label: Todd Lawson — The Crucifixion and the Qur'an
receipts.note: Argues tafsir, not bare Qur'anic wording, hardens into categorical denial.

receipts.label: AJIS — Revisiting the Crucifixion within Islam
receipts.note: Documents non-monolithic Muslim positions, including Isma'ili affirmation.

receipts.label: Qur'an 3:55; 19:33
receipts.note: Verses used in internal Muslim debate about Jesus' death and raising.

arguments.crux: Does Qur'an 4:157 deny the historical occurrence of Jesus' crucifixion, or only the claim that his opponents successfully killed God's messenger?

arguments.title: The "Islamic dilemma" (Qur'an affirms the Bible)

christian.claim: The Qur'an tells Jews and Christians to judge by the Torah and Gospel they possess; if those books affirm Christian essentials that Islam rejects, Muslims face a dilemma: accept the Bible and contradict Islam, or reject the Bible and contradict the Qur'an.
christian.case: Common proof-texts: 5:43–47, 5:68, 10:94, 3:3–4, 5:48. Christian apologists argue 7th-century Torah/Gospel content is substantially continuous with today's Bible, so "corruption after Muhammad" cannot rescue the dilemma.

receipts.label: Qur'an 5:47
receipts.note: Let the People of the Gospel judge by what God has revealed therein.

receipts.label: Qur'an 10:94
receipts.note: Directs the doubter to ask prior scripture readers.

receipts.label: Catholic Answers — Bible corruption?
receipts.note: Popular Christian presentation of the dilemma.

receipts.label: Reynolds — JAOS on tahrif
receipts.note: Academic analysis of Qur'anic falsification language.

response.claim: The Qur'an affirms earlier revelation as divine in origin while criticizing misinterpretation, concealment, and later theological accretions; "Injil" need not mean the four canonical Gospels as closed Christian dogma.
response.case: Abdullah Saeed maps Muslim positions on prior scriptures and notes Qur'anic reverence for Tawrat/Injil alongside critique of those who distort words from their places (4:46; 5:13; 5:41) — often read first as tahrif al-ma'na (distort meaning). The Qur'an is muhaymin (5:48) over prior books. Affirmation is not a blank check for every later Christian doctrine. Classical Muslims disagree on how much textual change occurred.

receipts.label: Abdullah Saeed — Charge of Distortion
receipts.note: Major Muslim scholarly treatment of tahrif.

receipts.label: Qur'an 5:48
receipts.note: Qur'an as guardian/criterion (muhaymin) over previous scripture.

receipts.label: MDPI Religions — Abrogation or Confirmation?
receipts.note: Argues Qur'an presents itself as confirmer (musaddiq) more than abrogator.

arguments.crux: When the Qur'an says "Gospel," does it mean the Christian canon's doctrinal content as Christians define it, or an earlier revelation the Qur'an claims to confirm and correct?

arguments.title: Trinity as shirk (associating partners with God)

christian.claim: Orthodox Trinity is monotheism (one being, three persons), so Islamic charges of tritheism attack a straw man; Qur'anic polemics often miss the doctrine Christians actually hold.
christian.case: Christians cite the Shema plus NT worship of Jesus. They argue Q 5:116 and Q 5:73 do not describe Nicene orthodoxy. Therefore Islam's rejection is misaimed or still rejects biblical revelation of God.

receipts.label: Qur'an 5:72–73; 5:116
receipts.note: Primary Qur'anic polemics against "third of three" / Jesus and Mary as gods.

receipts.label: Christian Century — Allah and the Trinity
receipts.note: Argues Qur'anic rejections often target misconceptions, not classical Trinity.

receipts.label: Nicene Creed
receipts.note: Canonical Christian definition: one God; Son consubstantial with the Father.

response.claim: Even the carefully stated Nicene Trinity still ascribes deity and worship to Jesus, which the Qur'an classifies as shirk regardless of "one essence" language.
response.case: Islamic tawhid is absolute unpartitioned oneness. Ibn Taymiyya and later theologians argue that if Father, Son, and Spirit are each fully God, reason yields multiple divinities. Qur'an 4:171: say not "Three." The dispute is definitional: what counts as monotheism?

receipts.label: Qur'an 4:171
receipts.note: Do not say "Three"… God is only one God.

receipts.label: Qur'an 112 (al-Ikhlas)
receipts.note: God is One, begets not, is not begotten.

receipts.label: Erickson — Islamic Monotheism and the Trinity
receipts.note: Documents Muslim philosophical critique of Trinity.

arguments.crux: Is "one being / three persons" still monotheism, or is any worship of Jesus already shirk by definition?

arguments.title: Jesus' deity and divine sonship

christian.claim: Earliest Christian sources present Jesus as receiving worship and divine status; Islam's purely human messenger-Christ is a later theological downgrade.
christian.case: Christians appeal to Philippians 2:6–11, John 1:1–14, John 20:28, and early high Christology. They argue Muhammad, six centuries later, cannot overturn apostolic-linked testimony.

receipts.label: Philippians 2:6–11
receipts.note: Early Christian hymn language of exaltation.

receipts.label: John 20:28
receipts.note: Thomas: My Lord and my God!

receipts.label: Qur'an 5:72; 19:35
receipts.note: Denies divinity of Jesus; God does not take a son.

response.claim: Jesus in the Qur'an is Messiah, word, and spirit from God — exalted but created; later Christian creeds developed beyond Jesus' own monotheistic preaching.
response.case: Muslims cite Qur'an 3:45–51; 4:171; 5:75 and Gospel sayings read as unitarian (Mark 12:29; John 17:3). "Son of God" in Semitic idiom can mean favored servant; metaphysical sonship is treated as later development. The Qur'an claims to restore Jesus' actual message against church doctrine.

receipts.label: Qur'an 4:171
receipts.note: Jesus is messenger, word cast to Mary, spirit from God — not a third of three.

receipts.label: Qur'an 3:45–51
receipts.note: High regard for Jesus with explicit creaturely limits.

receipts.label: Mark 12:29 / John 17:3
receipts.note: Texts Muslims frequently cite for Jesus affirming one God.

arguments.crux: Did Jesus claim or receive the kind of deity Nicene Christianity ascribes — and is later revelation allowed to adjudicate that question?

arguments.title: Muhammad as false prophet

christian.claim: By biblical tests of prophecy (and/or by moral-historical critique), Muhammad fails as a prophet from the God of Abraham.
christian.case: Common lines: (1) Deut 18's prophet like Moses is an Israelite with face-to-face communion and signs — said to fit Jesus, not Muhammad; (2) denying crucifixion/deity contradicts prior revelation; (3) Satanic verses reports used as false-revelation evidence; (4) warfare vs Jesus' pattern.

receipts.label: Deuteronomy 18:15–22
receipts.note: Prophet-like-Moses passage and false-prophet tests used by both sides.

receipts.label: CRI — Muhammad and Deuteronomy 18
receipts.note: Christian critique of Muslim use of Deut 18.

receipts.label: Wood — Deuteronomy Deductions
receipts.note: Uses Satanic verses reports plus Deut 18 to argue false prophecy.

receipts.label: Qur'an 7:157
receipts.note: Claims the unlettered prophet is mentioned in Torah and Gospel with them.

response.claim: Muhammad fits the Mosaic pattern as lawgiver-statesman more closely than Jesus, is foretold in prior scripture, and is validated by the Qur'an's challenge and mass transmission — while Satanic verses reports are weak or a test he passed.
response.case: Muslim apologetics stress Moses/Muhammad parallels as lawgivers and community leaders. Internal criteria: i'jaz (inimitability), tawhid consistency, character. Many Muslims dispute Satanic verses authenticity; others say any interference was blocked (22:52 debate).

receipts.label: Qur'an 17:88; 2:23
receipts.note: Challenge verses used as internal proof of prophethood.

receipts.label: Qur'an 61:6
receipts.note: Jesus said to foretell a messenger after him named Ahmad.

receipts.label: SBJT — Does the Bible predict Muhammad?
receipts.note: Maps Christian counters to Muslim Deut/Paraclete arguments.

receipts.label: Qur'an 22:52
receipts.note: Discussed in debates on prophetic protection from satanic interference.

arguments.crux: Which revelation's prophet-tests are authoritative — and must a true prophet agree with Nicene Christianity?

arguments.title: Qur'an preservation vs Bible manuscripts

christian.claim: The Qur'an's perfect-preservation claim is overstated: Uthman standardized the text and destroyed rivals, and multiple qira'at remain; the NT manuscript tradition is earlier and denser.
christian.case: Christian apologists cite Sahih al-Bukhari on Uthman's commission and burning of other materials, plus modern manuscript work on variants, to argue a double standard in Muslim attacks on biblical textual history.

receipts.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 4987
receipts.note: Classic hadith report of Uthmanic standardization and destruction of other copies.

receipts.label: 1517 — Perfectly Preserved?
receipts.note: Christian apologetic summary of modern Qur'anic textual research pressures.

receipts.label: TGC — Countering Muslim attacks on the Bible
receipts.note: Turns corruption charge back toward Qur'anic canon history.

response.claim: Uthmanic standardization preserved a mutawatir consonantal skeleton already orally mass-transmitted; qira'at are authorized recitation modes within that rasm, not rival Qur'ans.
response.case: Muslim scholarship argues companions agreed on the rasm; variants that contradicted it were treated as abrogated, commentary, or error. Comparative claim: biblical books have anonymous authorship debates and doctrinally meaningful variants, whereas Qur'anic differences are mostly recitational within an accepted range.

receipts.label: Yaqeen — The Uthmanic Codex
receipts.note: Detailed account of what standardization did and did not remove.

receipts.label: Qur'an 15:9
receipts.note: Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian.

receipts.label: TAFASIR — Authenticity of Mushaf Uthmani
receipts.note: Recent Muslim academic defense of Uthmanic authenticity.

arguments.crux: Are qira'at and the Uthmanic project evidence of corruption, or of controlled preservation of an oral-written revelation?

arguments.title: Islam and violence / jihad

christian.claim: Islamic scripture and classical law authorize religious warfare in ways that make violence structural, not merely aberrant.
christian.case: Evangelical critiques cite sword verses (9:5; 9:29; 8:12; 8:39), Maghazi warfare in the sirah, and classical offensive jihad doctrines. They distinguish peaceful Muslims from what they call non-peaceful source texts.

receipts.label: Qur'an 9:5; 9:29
receipts.note: Frequently cited sword and jizya verses in Christian critique.

receipts.label: NAMB — Islam and Violence
receipts.note: Evangelical overview arguing jihad is a clear component of the tradition.

receipts.label: CRI — Is Islam a Religion of Peace?
receipts.note: Popular maximalist Christian critique.

response.claim: Permission to fight in the Qur'an is primarily defensive, constrained by non-aggression and non-combatant protections; extremist violence violates classical limits.
response.case: Muslim responses emphasize 22:39–40 and 2:190 (fight those who fight you, do not transgress). Tafsir traditions prohibit killing women, children, monks. Honest map note: classical tradition also contains expansionist jihad theories — this is an intra-Islamic dispute too.

receipts.label: Qur'an 2:190; 22:39–40
receipts.note: Core defensive-war proof-texts in Muslim apologetics.

receipts.label: EJIL — The Use of Force under Islamic Law
receipts.note: Legal-academic treatment of defensive vs offensive jihad theories.

receipts.label: Tafheem on 2:190
receipts.note: Modern tafsir explaining non-transgression limits in war.

receipts.label: First Things — Challenging Radical Islam
receipts.note: Notes classical limits against targeting civilians.

arguments.crux: Do the Medinan war verses authorize enduring offensive holy war, or context-bound defense under ethical limits?

arguments.title: Apostasy punishment

christian.claim: Traditional Islamic law's death penalty for apostasy is incompatible with genuine religious freedom and with Jesus' ethic.
christian.case: Christian critics cite hadith such as "Whoever changes his religion, kill him" (Bukhari) and classical hudud treatment of ridda, contrasting this with the NT's lack of a civil death penalty for leaving the faith.

receipts.label: Sahih al-Bukhari 6922
receipts.note: Often cited hadith on killing the one who leaves Islam.

receipts.label: Probe — Islam and Christianity misconceptions
receipts.note: Representative popular Christian framing on liberty themes.

response.claim: Classical apostasy law was largely about treason against the Muslim polity; many contemporary Muslim scholars reject capital punishment for mere private belief change.
response.case: Reformers and some classical nuances argue 2:256 (no compulsion in religion) and 18:29 protect conscience. Ridda wars under Abu Bakr are read as political rebellion. Map note: traditional madhhab manuals do prescribe death for adult male apostates — so this response is partly reformist, not unanimous heritage.

receipts.label: Qur'an 2:256
receipts.note: There is no compulsion in religion.

receipts.label: Qur'an 18:29
receipts.note: Let who will believe, and let who will disbelieve.

receipts.label: Qur'an 4:137
receipts.note: Used in debates about whether apostasy is a fixed capital hadd.

arguments.crux: Is capital punishment for apostasy required by Islam's sources, or a contingent legal doctrine that can be rejected without leaving Islam?

arguments.title: Women, polygamy, and legal inequality

christian.claim: Islamic law institutionalizes male authority and unequal rights (polygyny, testimony, inheritance, discipline verse) contrary to the dignity Jesus modeled toward women.
christian.case: Critics highlight Qur'an 4:3, 4:11, 2:282, 4:34, and historical practices. They contrast Gospel narratives of Jesus teaching women and appearing first to women witnesses of resurrection.

receipts.label: Qur'an 4:3; 4:34; 4:11
receipts.note: Primary verses in Christian critiques of gender hierarchy.

receipts.label: Probe — gender and comparative roles
receipts.note: Popular evangelical contrast on gender roles.

response.claim: Qur'anic rules reformed 7th-century Arabia toward women's rights; polygyny is restricted conditional permission; 4:34 is contested in interpretation; Christian history also embeds patriarchy.
response.case: Muslim responses stress property rights, consent in marriage, exalted status of mothers, and justice conditions on polygyny (4:3; 4:129). Many modern scholars reject abusive readings of 4:34. Comparative reply: OT polygyny and long Christian institutional patriarchy complicate simple Jesus-vs-Islam contrasts.

receipts.label: Qur'an 4:129
receipts.note: Warns you will not be able to deal justly between wives.

receipts.label: Qur'an 33:35
receipts.note: Parallel spiritual address to believing men and women.

receipts.label: Qur'an 4:32
receipts.note: For men a share of what they earn, and for women a share of what they earn.

arguments.crux: Are the contested gender rulings timeless unequal ontology, or historically situated law aiming at justice that can be re-read as norms change?

arguments.title: Salvation: grace through Christ vs deeds and mercy

christian.claim: Christianity offers assurance through Christ's atoning death; Islam offers a scale of deeds plus hope in mercy without substitutionary atonement, leaving sinners without a sufficient remedy.
christian.case: Evangelical contrast (e.g. Nabeel Qureshi): humans need perfect righteousness; only Christ's cross provides it. Islam's denial of crucifixion removes the atonement mechanism.

receipts.label: Romans 3:21–26; 1 John 5:13
receipts.note: Core Christian atonement/assurance texts used in contrast.

receipts.label: RTS review — No God but One (Qureshi)
receipts.note: Summarizes a widely used convert-apologist framing of the salvation contrast.

response.claim: Islam rejects inherited sin and vicarious atonement as unjust; God forgives by repentance (tawba), faith, and mercy without needing a crucified deity.
response.case: Qur'an 39:53; 53:38–39; 2:286. Muslims argue moral responsibility is individual; the Christian cross raises its own justice problem (innocent punished). Mercy (rahma) is decisive.

receipts.label: Qur'an 53:38–39
receipts.note: No soul bears another's burden; man has only what he strives for.

receipts.label: Qur'an 39:53
receipts.note: Do not despair of God's mercy… He forgives all sins.

receipts.label: Qur'an 4:48
receipts.note: God does not forgive shirk if one dies upon it, but forgives what is less than that for whom He wills.

arguments.crux: Is forgiveness without substitutionary atonement morally sufficient — or is the cross necessary for both justice and assurance?
